01.actor: The daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Guryon
01.event: The Sages allotted the widowed daughter-in-law of Nakdimon ben Guryon two se'a of wine a week for cooking, and she blessed them that they should allot the same to their own daughters.
01.turn: She was a widow waiting for her yavam, so her blessing implied wishing her plight on their daughters.
01.outcome: The Sages did not answer amen to her blessing.
01.summary: After her husband died, the Sages granted the daughter-in-law of the wealthy Nakdimon ben Guryon two se'a of wine every week for her cooking. Grateful, she blessed them: may you allot the same to your daughters. But she was a widow bound to her brother-in-law, so the Sages refused to answer amen, not wanting their daughters to end up in her situation.

02.actor: The sister of Rami bar Hama and her husband Rav Avya
02.event: The marriage contract of Rami bar Hama's sister, wife of Rav Avya, was lost and the couple came before Rav Yosef.
02.turn: Rav Yosef cited Shmuel that the ruling forbidding a couple without a full marriage contract is only Rabbi Meir's view.
02.summary: Rami bar Hama's sister was married to Rav Avya. Her marriage contract was lost, and the couple went to Rav Yosef to ask what to do. He told them that the view that such a couple may not live together belongs to Rabbi Meir.
02.missing: The passage itself is only the introductory line; the problem comes in the next segment, and the final ruling for the couple is not shown.

04.event: Walking on the road with a woman ahead of them, Rav urged Rav Yehuda to hurry away from her.
04.turn: Rav Yehuda objected that Rav himself permitted it for men of fit morals, and Rav answered that he did not mean men like themselves.
04.outcome: Rav clarified he meant only men like Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues.
04.summary: Rav and his student Rav Yehuda were travelling when a woman was walking ahead of them. Rav told him to speed up and escape 'Gehenna' rather than be secluded with her. Rav Yehuda reminded him that he had ruled it permitted for upright men; Rav answered that he did not mean the likes of the two of them, but only proven saints such as Rabbi Hanina bar Pappi and his colleagues.

05.actor: A man who betrothed a woman with stolen coins
05.event: A man snatched coins from someone and threw them to a woman washing her feet, declaring her betrothed to him.
05.turn: The case came before Rava, who held that the owner of stolen money is not presumed to have given up on it.
05.summary: A woman was washing her feet in a basin when a man grabbed some coins from another person, threw them to her, and said 'You are betrothed to me.' The matter came before Rava, who ruled that no one follows Rabbi Shimon's view that a robbery victim gives up on his money; the coins were not the man's, so the betrothal did not take effect.

06.event: A man let witnesses trace their names on ordinary financial documents.
06.turn: That leniency applied only to bills of divorce.
06.summary: Someone applied the leniency of letting illiterate witnesses trace their signatures to ordinary financial documents, not just bills of divorce. Rav Kahana had him flogged for it.
06.missing: It is a one-line report; who the person was and the circumstances are not given.

07.actor: A man who came before Rabban Gamliel
07.event: A man complained to Rabban Gamliel that he found his bride without signs of virginity.
07.turn: Rabban Gamliel suggested he had diverted his approach, illustrating with a parable of a door found open or locked.
07.summary: A man came to Rabban Gamliel claiming he had found his bride's opening unobstructed. Rabban Gamliel suggested that perhaps he had come at it at an angle (or, in another version, forced it), and compared him to a man in the dark who finds a door open or locked depending on whether he moves the bolt.
07.missing: How the case was resolved is not stated.

08.actor: A herdsman for orphans and a creditor
08.event: A creditor seized an ox from a herdsman caring for orphans' cattle, and they disputed whether he seized it before or after the debtor's death.
08.turn: Rav Nahman asked whether there were witnesses to the seizure, and there were none.
08.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the creditor, since he could have claimed he bought it, he is believed that he seized it during the debtor's lifetime.
08.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman who looked after some orphans' cattle, to pay their late father's debt. The creditor said he took it while the father was alive; the herdsman said it was after his death. Rav Nahman asked the herdsman whether anyone saw the seizure; no one had, so he ruled that the creditor, who could have claimed to have bought the ox, is believed.

09.event: During a famine in Rav Yosef's time, the Sages asked him to pray for mercy.
09.turn: He refused, pointing out that even Elisha, who supported 2,200 scholars, did not pray in a time of divine anger.
09.summary: In Rav Yosef's day there was a famine seen as divine anger, and the Sages asked him to pray. He declined, arguing that if Elisha, who fed 2,200 scholars, did not pray at such a time, he should not either.
09.missing: What happened after his refusal is not shown.

10.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his weekly four dinars for a poor man via his wife.
10.turn: She overheard the household asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths and concluded he did not need charity.
10.outcome: Rabbi Hanina responded by citing Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers, since they excuse our failings toward the truly poor.
10.summary: Rabbi Hanina used to send four dinars to a certain poor man every Friday. One week he sent his wife, who came back saying the man did not need it: she had overheard his family asking whether he would dine on the silver or the gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina remarked, quoting Rabbi Elazar, that we should appreciate swindlers, because without them we would be guilty every day of neglecting the real poor.

11.actor: A betrothed couple before Rav Yosef
11.event: A pregnant betrothed woman and her fiance came before Rav Yosef; she said the child was his.
11.turn: He confirmed that it was his.
11.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled there was no concern, since the man admitted paternity and in any case the halakha follows Rabban Gamliel.
11.summary: A betrothed woman became pregnant before the wedding, and she and her fiance came to Rav Yosef. She said she had conceived from him, and he agreed. Rav Yosef ruled there was nothing to worry about: the man admitted it, and the law trusts her claim anyway.

13.event: Ravina, holding his orphaned nephew's wine, was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell.
13.turn: He asked Rav Ashi whether he could take the orphan's wine along.
13.outcome: Rav Ashi told him to go, since the orphan's wine needs no better treatment than his own.
13.summary: Ravina was looking after wine belonging to his orphaned nephew, Ravina the younger, and was taking his own wine to Sikhra to sell. He asked Rav Ashi whether he could bring the orphan's wine too. Rav Ashi told him to go ahead: the orphan's wine deserved no better than his own.

14.event: Shimon ben Azzai found a lineage scroll in Jerusalem.
14.turn: It recorded that a certain man was a mamzer, that Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov's teachings were few but sound, and that Manasseh killed Isaiah.
14.summary: Shimon ben Azzai reported finding a genealogical scroll in Jerusalem. It recorded that a certain person was a mamzer, praised Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov's teachings as small but clean, and stated that King Manasseh killed the prophet Isaiah.
14.missing: It is a report of a find and its contents; nothing follows from the discovery within the passage.

16.event: A marriage contract with a recognized scribal formula and one verified witness signature came before Rabbi Abbahu.
16.turn: Rabbi Abbahu intended to validate it, but Rabbi Yirmeya objected that the scribe must have signed, not merely written it.
16.outcome: Rabbi Yirmeya's correction stood against validating it.
16.summary: A marriage contract was brought to Rabbi Abbahu; people recognized the scribe's handwriting and one witness's signature. Rabbi Abbahu was inclined to accept it on that basis. Rabbi Yirmeya stopped him: the law speaks of a scribe who signed, and his handwriting alone is not enough.
16.missing: Whether Rabbi Abbahu then rejected the document is implied, not stated.

17.event: Rav Kahana, a priest, took a cloth as redemption for a firstborn son and declared that to him it was worth five sela.
17.outcome: The redemption was accepted on his valuation.
17.summary: When a man had to redeem his firstborn son, Rav Kahana, a priest, took a cloth from his house instead of five silver coins, saying that to him the cloth was worth five sela.
17.missing: It is cited as a brief precedent; the second report (Mar bar Rav Ashi buying a cloth) is a separate one-line illustration.

18.event: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi summoned his younger son Rabbi Shimon and passed him the orders of wisdom, then his older son Rabban Gamliel and passed him the procedures of the patriarchate.
18.turn: He divided his legacy, and instructed Rabban Gamliel to rule assertively and instill fear in the students.
18.summary: As he was dying, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked for his younger son, Rabbi Shimon, and handed him the teachings of wisdom. Then he asked for his elder son, Rabban Gamliel, gave him the procedures of the office of Nasi, and told him to lead with a firm hand and keep the students in awe.
18.missing: The beginning of the deathbed narrative and its end (his death) lie outside the segments shown.

19.actor: A man who came before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
19.event: A man testified to Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that someone was a Levite because he was called second to the Torah.
19.turn: Asked whether that might reflect prominence rather than lineage, he answered that a priest had read before him.
19.outcome: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi granted the man Levite status on that testimony.
19.summary: A man told Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi that he had seen someone established as a Levite, because he was called second to the Torah in synagogue. The rabbi asked whether he was called as a Levite or merely as an important man; the witness replied that a priest had read just before him. On that basis Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi recognized the man as a Levite.

20.event: The Sages asked Rabbi Abbahu, in riddling language, where Rabbi Elai was hiding.
20.turn: He answered in a riddle that Elai had taken a lively young wife of priestly family who had kept him awake.
20.summary: The Sages, speaking in wordplay, asked Rabbi Abbahu where Rabbi Elai had disappeared to. He answered in a riddle of his own: Elai had married a lively young woman of priestly descent, his second wife, and she had kept him up all night.
20.missing: It is a single exchange of wit; nothing further happens.
